overview.text: Bone, also called osseous tissue, is hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton. Individual bones—such as the femur, ribs, and skull bones—support the body, provide levers moved by muscles at joints, and protect organs including the brain, heart, and lungs. Bone’s matrix combines collagen fibers with mineral crystals, giving it strength and some flexibility. Living bone is continually remodeled as bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts work in balance. Most bones contain dense compact tissue and lighter, lattice-like spongy tissue. Spongy bone can contain red marrow, which produces blood cells; marrow can also store fat. Bones additionally store and release minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus.

key_facts.text: Compact bone is organized into osteons, with central Haversian canals that carry blood vessels and nerves.
Spongy bone is a lattice of trabeculae; its spaces make bone lighter, and some contain red marrow.
Osteoblasts form bone, osteoclasts break it down, and osteocytes are mature bone cells; their activity helps maintain and remodel bone tissue.
Red marrow produces blood cells, while yellow marrow contains fat used for energy storage.
Bone stores minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus, and can release them into the bloodstream.
